issues.failure_explanation: The paper defines ||y~(t)||/||y(t)|| = 1+xi(t) and takes t~* with ||y~(t~*)|| = 0.5. It follows that ||y(t~*)|| = 0.5/(1+xi(t~*)). The text instead writes ||y(t~*)|| = 0.5(1+xi(t~*)). This contradicts the preceding definition and the paper's own numbers: a ratio of 2.3882 gives ||y|| ≈ 0.209, not 0.5·2.3882. The two quantities are also swapped relative to the t* statement. The bound |xi| ≤ delta then does not give the stated range for ||y(t~*)||, and for delta > 1 the lower side is not bounded by 1-delta.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the display by ||y(t~*)|| = 0.5/(1+xi(t~*)) and restate the resulting range (1+xi ≥ 1-delta, with care when delta ≥ 1).
issues.overall_effect: The motivating argument that delta(t) controls the error in the end-of-transient time rests on an incorrect formula. The numerical example itself is unaffected.
issues.title: Wrong relation between ||y(t~*)|| and ||y~(t~*)|| in building-heating discussion
issues.why_classification: A local one-line correction restores the argument; all numerical results and conclusions are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Using the Euclidean norm as vector norm, we have $V_1=0.9988$ and $W_1=0.9986$.

issues.failure_explanation: The onset condition (epsilonc<) contains the term (1/2)log(1/(1-V_1)), which comes from the factor 2/sqrt(1-V_1). With V_1≈0.9988 this term is about 3.36. The example instead evaluates (1/2)log(1/sqrt(1-V_1)) ≈ 1.68, which is half the correct value. The reported number is therefore not the quantity in the cited bound, and the comparison with log(f_2/f_1)=-2.81 used to explain the quick onset is distorted.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use (1/2)log(1/(1-V_1)) ≈ 3.36, recompute the combined onset time from (epsilonc<), and restate the comparison.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical explanation of why the onset is fast in this example understates the V_1-delay by a factor 2. The qualitative conclusion is not overturned.
issues.title: Example 7.6: onset term uses (1/2)log(1/sqrt(1-V_1)) instead of the (1/2)log(1/(1-V_1)) from the onset bound

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In the vast majority of cases for (\ref{ode}), the relative error of the perturbed initial value is magnified in the perturbed solution
The mathematical results of the paper, included in Sections 3 to 6, analyze the asymptotic (long-time) behavior

issues.failure_explanation: Sections 3-6 prove only the asymptotic statements (K ~ K_inf and onset bounds). The claim that max K and max K_inf have the same order 'in the vast majority of cases' rests solely on Monte Carlo tests for specific Gaussian ensembles. These use 10000 samples, T equal to 50 characteristic times, and p in {1,2,infinity}. The Conclusion states it as 'the main result' for arbitrary real ODEs. The tables also contradict 'never much larger than 1'. R reaches 7.49 for the infinity-norm, R is as small as 7e-4 (K_inf far above max K), and the non-normal ensemble gives R up to 502. No theorem bounds max K by a multiple of K_inf, and the complex-rightmost case further requires V_1 not close to 1.

failure_location.quote: Indeed, it is never much larger than $1$ in these $10\ 000$ instances.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the claim explicitly as an empirical observation for the tested random ensembles, with the observed spread of R (including values far above and below 1). Drop 'main result' and 'never much larger', or supply a proof of the comparability.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised main result, and the Section 9 transfer of E to E_inf, are heuristic observations restricted to the sampled ensembles. They are not established results about 'the vast majority' of ODEs.
issues.title: Empirical findings presented as a 'main result'; 'never much larger than 1' contradicts the paper's own tables
issues.why_classification: The rigorous content is untouched and the fix is a rewording plus honest quantification. But the headline claim loses its status as a result, which is a limited weakening of what the paper advertises.
